title: Hillrose Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hillrose wells have a median depth of 82 feet, with typical completed-well costs of $8,900-$16,500.
h1: What Hillrose Well Records Tell Land Buyers
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Hillrose show a shallow plains setting, with a median reported well depth of 82 feet. Most recorded wells are domestic, stock, or irrigation wells, and the available yield records generally point to strong production. That does not guarantee the result on a particular lot. A permit record describes a nearby well, not the exact conditions under your proposed house.

The practical questions are depth, production, water quality, and total installation cost. Hillrose records also show limited static-water-level reporting, so buyers should treat the water-level picture as useful but incomplete. Before closing or starting construction, review the nearest well permits, confirm the intended use, and plan for septic, access, electrical service, and water testing.

sections.heading: Hillrose wells are usually shallow
sections.html:
The middle half of recorded well depths runs from 66 to 95 feet, with a median of 82 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling estimate in Hillrose. The depth distribution is concentrated near the surface: 79% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 20% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The deepest recorded well is 460 feet, so shallow ground is common but not guaranteed.

Local geology helps explain the spread. Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer conditions for 728 wells, while only 5 identify Quaternary Alluvium and 5 identify Alluvial conditions. A driller still needs to evaluate the exact lot, access, casing and grout requirements, and nearby completion records before giving a firm bid.

sections.heading: Production is generally strong, but verify the specific lot
sections.html:
Only 130 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield sample is much smaller than the total permit file. Within that sample, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 974.8 gallons per minute, and 88% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Twelve percent report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 1% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute.

No reported well is listed under 1 gallon per minute in this yield sample. Even so, a high nearby yield does not promise the same result on a new hole. Ask for the closest constructed wells, their completion depths, pump tests, and intended household demand. Storage and pump sizing also matter, not just the reported gallons-per-minute figure.

sections.heading: Hillrose water levels look shallow, but the trend is not proven
sections.html:
Just 24 wells report a static water level, so the water-level data should not be treated as a complete neighborhood survey. Among those reports, the median depth to water is 18 feet, and the middle half runs from 11 to 19 feet. That suggests water is commonly encountered relatively near the surface in the reported wells.

The permit records supplied here do not provide a water-level series by decade. Because of that, they do not establish that the water table is dropping or stable over time. A buyer should ask about the date and conditions of any static-water measurement, then confirm current performance with a well test. Shallow groundwater also makes proper casing, grout, wellhead protection, and septic separation important.

sections.heading: Hillrose permit history includes long-established local drillers
sections.html:
Hillrose has a long permit history, with records issued from the 1950s through the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2024. Canfield Drilling Company, also listed as Canfield, Harold E, appears on 110 records. Canfield, Leslie George appears on 61, and Brunkhardt Water Well Drilling, listed as Brunkhardt, Robert J, appears on 26.

Those names help identify local drilling history, but a permit count is not a recommendation and does not show current availability. When comparing a bid, ask who will perform the work, what casing and grout are included, how the well will be developed and tested, and how unsuccessful drilling is handled. DWR permit requirements and the authorized use should also match your building plans.

sections.heading: A Hillrose well budget starts near the shallow-depth median
sections.html:
The local drilling model uses a typical rate of $35-$55 per foot for alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 82-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $2,900-$4,500. That is not the finished water system. Pump equipment, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work bring the estimated completed-well range to about $8,900-$16,500.

Use the drilling figure as one line in a larger site budget. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, rocky conditions, long utility runs, or an unusual pump setup can change the final price. Get a written scope that separates drilling, casing, testing, pump installation, trenching, electrical, and permit-related work before relying on a low per-foot number.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic layout, and dry-hole risk
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. There are no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the supplied records. That does not establish whether a particular well is safe. Test the well water before purchase and again after construction or a significant change in use, with the panel selected for local conditions and the intended household use.

Low yield and dry holes remain site-specific risks even where nearby records look favorable. Have the driller review neighboring permits before mobilizing. On a building lot, reserve room for the wellhead, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and utility trenching. An exempt household-use well still has limits, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be needed in an over-appropriated basin.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hillrose, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth within 5 miles of Hillrose is 82 feet. The middle half runs from 66 to 95 feet, and 79% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Some are deeper: 20% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and the deepest record is 460 feet. Nearby depth records are a guide, not a guarantee for a new lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hillrose?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 82-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $2,900-$4,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $8,900-$16,500. A bid can change with access, depth, casing, grout, pump size, and site conditions.

faq.q: How much water do Hillrose wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 130 Hillrose-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. Eighty-eight percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 12% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute and 1% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. The yield sample is limited, so test the specific well before relying on it.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Hillrose?
faq.a: The records do not prove that any individual Hillrose well is safe to drink. There are 8 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles, so testing deserves specific attention. Test before purchase and after construction, using a laboratory panel suited to the property. Proper casing, grout, wellhead protection, and septic placement also matter.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Hillrose?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a falling water table. Only 24 wells report static water levels, with a median depth to water of 18 feet and a middle half from 11 to 19 feet. The supplied data has no water-level series by decade. Ask for current measurements and a well test rather than assuming the limited records show a long-term trend.
